title: Async JavaScript and fetch
intro: Web applications constantly wait for things outside the JavaScript code itself: network responses, timers, user actions, and other browser work. In this lesson, you will learn how asynchronous JavaScript works, how Promises and async/await make it manageable, and how React applications can handle API loading and error states.
takeaways: Asynchronous JavaScript lets the browser continue handling other work while timers, network requests, and other operations finish later.
Promises represent pending, fulfilled, or rejected asynchronous operations, while async/await provides a readable way to consume them.
fetch() does not reject just because an HTTP response has a 4xx or 5xx status, so check response.ok explicitly.
Use JSON.stringify() for JSON request bodies and response.json() to parse JSON response data.
Real applications should represent loading, success, and error states, and independent requests can often run together with Promise.all().

quiz.question: What does an async function return?
options: The value before asynchronous work finishes
quiz.explanation: An async function always returns a Promise. A returned normal value becomes the fulfilled value of that Promise.

quiz.question: What should you normally check after calling fetch() to detect an HTTP 404 or 500 response?
quiz.explanation: fetch() normally resolves even for HTTP error statuses, so response.ok should be checked before treating the response as successful.

quiz.question: What does this code do? `const [users, products] = await Promise.all([loadUsers(), loadProducts()]);`
options: Runs loadUsers(), waits for it, then starts loadProducts()
Starts both operations and waits for both to fulfill
quiz.explanation: Both functions are called when the Promise.all array is created, so their asynchronous work can proceed together. Promise.all then waits for both results.

quiz.question: What does `await response.json()` give you when the response contains valid JSON representing an array of users?
quiz.explanation: response.json() returns a Promise that parses the response body as JSON. Awaiting it gives you the corresponding JavaScript value, such as an array of user objects.

quiz.question: Which Promise state means that an asynchronous operation has completed successfully?
quiz.explanation: A fulfilled Promise represents successful completion. Pending means it has not settled yet, while rejected represents failure.

exercise.title: Load and time out asynchronous data
exercise.task: Implement exactly two functions: `loadUserNames(fetchFn)` and `withTimeout(promise, ms)`. `loadUserNames(fetchFn)` must call `fetchFn("/api/users")`, throw `new Error("Request failed: " + status)` when the response has `ok === false`, otherwise await `response.json()` and return the user names sorted alphabetically. `withTimeout(promise, ms)` must settle with the original Promise's result when it settles first, but reject with `new Error("Timeout")` when the given Promise has not settled within the specified number of milliseconds. The tests provide fake fetch functions and Promises, so do not make real network requests.
exercise.hint: For `loadUserNames`, await the fake fetch function, check `response.ok`, then await `response.json()`, map the users to their names, and sort the resulting array. For `withTimeout`, create a Promise that rejects with the exact `Timeout` error after `ms` milliseconds and race it against the supplied Promise with `Promise.race()`.

tests.name: Loads and sorts user names
tests.code: const fakeFetch = async url => ({ ok: true, status: 200, json: async () => [{ name: "Zoe" }, { name: "Anna" }, { name: "Peter" }] }); const names = await loadUserNames(fakeFetch); return JSON.stringify(names) === JSON.stringify(["Anna", "Peter", "Zoe"]);

tests.name: Calls the expected users endpoint
tests.code: let requestedUrl = null; const fakeFetch = async url => { requestedUrl = url; return { ok: true, status: 200, json: async () => [] }; }; await loadUserNames(fakeFetch); return requestedUrl === "/api/users";

tests.name: Throws the HTTP status error
tests.code: const fakeFetch = async () => ({ ok: false, status: 503, json: async () => [] }); try { await loadUserNames(fakeFetch); return false; } catch (error) { return error instanceof Error && error.message === "Request failed: 503"; }

tests.name: Returns the original promise result
tests.code: const result = await withTimeout(Promise.resolve("done"), 100); return result === "done";

tests.name: Times out a slow promise
tests.code: try { await withTimeout(new Promise(resolve => setTimeout(() => resolve("too late"), 80)), 10); return false; } catch (error) { return error instanceof Error && error.message === "Timeout"; }

tests.name: Preserves a rejection before the timeout
tests.code: try { await withTimeout(new Promise((_, reject) => setTimeout(() => reject(new Error("Original failure")), 10)), 100); return false; } catch (error) { return error instanceof Error && error.message === "Original failure"; }
